In episode 1039 of Syntax, a listener said he and his colleagues were producing more code with AI. His work increasingly felt like back-to-back PR reviews, and he found it exhausting.

It reminded me that generating code is one part of delivering a change.

When you implement a feature step by step, you build an understanding of the requirements, the data flow, and the boundaries of the change. When you receive AI-generated code, you may need to build that understanding afterward.

For example, an export feature might come together quickly. Someone still has to check that it exports the right data, handles failures correctly, and follows existing interface contracts.

Between answering questions, checking progress, and switching among several agents, the time saved during implementation can turn into more concentrated review and decision-making.

Teams face the same problem. If changes come in for review faster than the team can get through them, the backlog keeps growing.

The measure I care most about is how much time the team spends implementing, understanding, reviewing, and reworking a change from the initial request through delivery.

A few adjustments are worth trying.

- Give each change a clear purpose and a way to verify it. This makes it easier to review unfamiliar code in manageable pieces.
- Agree up front on how to handle routine decisions. That leaves more attention for important trade-offs and cuts down on repeated confirmations.
- Limit work in progress to what the team can review. Leave enough room to finish work that's already underway.

For a small, familiar change, implementing it directly can be efficient. How much AI contributes can vary by task.

What changes have made AI-assisted coding easier on your team?
